strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and relevant setting: neural multi-objective routing on asymmetric multigraphs, where both the next node and the connecting edge must be selected.

The two proposed architectures are complementary and well motivated: GMS-EB offers direct, context-dependent edge construction, while GMS-DH trades some expressiveness for substantially faster inference through learned pruning.

The methodology is clearly presented, including the preference-conditioned decoders, joint REINFORCE training for GMS-DH, complexity discussion, and an informative ablation of learned versus deterministic pruning.

The experimental study covers several problems, distributions, graph sizes, numbers of parallel edges, zero-shot generalization, runtime, training cost, and both neural and classical baselines. The models consistently outperform the tested neural and evolutionary baselines, with GMS-EB often within roughly 1–3% of LKH while being faster without augmentation.
The manuscript is readable, well organized, and candid about limitations such as GMS-EB's training cost and GMS-DH's context-independent edge selection.
weaknesses: The practical motivation is not validated empirically: all instances are synthetic, dense, complete graphs with independently generated attributes, and the multigraph distributions explicitly violate properties expected of real road networks. There are no real-world or established multigraph-routing benchmarks, and all tasks are bi-objective.

The most favorable result, MGMOTSPTW, lacks convincing baselines. The implicit LKH and OR-Tools variants ignore time windows, MBM uses an acknowledged simplistic pre-pruning rule, and the authors state that their custom evolutionary methods perform poorly. Comparison with a strong time-window-aware heuristic, adaptive large-neighborhood search, exact method on small instances, or another joint node/edge search procedure is needed.

The benefit of GMS-DH's central learned-pruning component is modest on MGMOTSP and is compelling only on one custom time-window setting with at most 50 nodes. Its fixed pre-route edge selection is also structurally unable to condition an edge choice on arrival time, load, or partial-route context, limiting the claimed general applicability.

There is no statistical uncertainty analysis: results appear to use a single training run, with no seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or paired tests. Many reported improvements are below 1–2%, so their significance cannot be assessed.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The preference distribution, Chebyshev ideal point, exact hypervolume normalization, hypernetwork architecture, clipping constant, random seeds, and several solver and local-search budgets are unspecified; code is only promised after acceptance.

Efficiency comparisons exclude the substantial training cost and compare GPU neural inference against parallel CPU heuristics. Augmented GMS-EB can also be slower than LKH, weakening broad speed claims.

At the component level, GMS-EB largely combines an existing edge GNN, multi-pointer decoder, and established multi-objective hypernetwork conditioning. GMS-DH is more distinctive, but the limited controlled evidence for learned pruning makes the overall novelty and empirical support slightly insufficient for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and largely unexplored setting: neural multi-objective routing on directed multigraphs. The edge-based and learned prune-then-route formulations are clear, technically plausible contributions rather than superficial extensions of node-based solvers.

The evaluation is broad for a neural combinatorial-optimization paper, covering four routing variants, several graph distributions and sizes, zero-shot generalization in both nodes and parallel edges, inference time, parameter counts, and training cost.

Results are consistently competitive: GMS substantially improves over the neural baseline on difficult asymmetric cases, approaches the much slower LKH baseline on additive problems, and performs especially well on the time-window variant. The quality-speed distinction between GMS-EB and GMS-DH is empirically useful.

The learned-pruning ablation, pre-pruning comparison, and simple-graph experiments help isolate architectural effects. The paper also reports unfavorable findings, including high training cost and cases where specialized Euclidean methods are better.
The presentation is generally clear, with coherent motivation, readable architecture diagrams, and useful implementation and problem details in the appendices.
weaknesses: The practical motivation is not validated empirically: every instance is synthetic and based mainly on dense complete graphs with independently sampled attributes. No real road-network multigraph, sparse structured graph, or operational routing dataset is included; the authors acknowledge that their multigraph distributions do not satisfy properties expected of real instances.

Evidence for the most distinctive claim—benefits from learned multigraph handling—is mixed. On MGMOTSP, exact preference-specific pruning is available, and learned pruning performs only marginally differently from simple post-encoding pruning. On the more compelling time-window problem, the comparison is less convincing because LKH and OR-Tools ignore time windows, MBM uses an ad hoc pruning rule and a different linear reward, and no strong problem-specific solver or optimality bound is provided.

Statistical reporting is insufficient for several small claimed improvements: results give means over test instances but no confidence intervals, paired tests, or variation across training seeds. Hypervolume is the sole quality metric, using manually selected reference points and an incompletely specified normalization, with no representative Pareto-front plots or complementary coverage metric.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the training preference distribution, ideal/utopian point used by the Chebyshev objective, full hypernetwork architecture, clipping constants, random seeds, checkpoint-selection procedure, and detailed LKH/OR-Tools configurations. Code is only promised after acceptance.

The computational burden is substantial—up to roughly 1.7 hours per epoch for GMS-EB before multiplying by hundreds of epochs—and the approach appears to require separately trained models across problems, distributions, and target sizes. Scalability is demonstrated only to 200 nodes, while the edge-based method has O(MN^4) decoding complexity.

The strongest recent multi-objective neural methods are compared only in the Euclidean appendix or discussed rather than adapted. Consequently, the main asymmetric and multigraph comparisons rely heavily on an author-constructed MBM baseline, limiting how decisively the experiments establish state-of-the-art performance.

The methodology is technically plausible and generally well explained, with equations, pseudocode, architecture details, and an explicit discussion of training cost and limitations.

The experiments are unusually broad, covering several routing problems, asymmetric distributions, graph sizes, parallel-edge counts, bi- and tri-objective settings, zero-shot scaling, and multiple heuristic, evolutionary, and neural baselines.
The learned-versus-simple-versus-pre-encoder pruning comparisons provide useful evidence that retaining the multigraph through the encoder can matter, especially for the time-window variant.
weaknesses: The central practical motivation is not validated: every experiment uses synthetic, dense, complete graphs, and the multigraph distributions are based on independent random edge attributes that generally violate the triangle inequality. There are no real-world, sparse, or established multigraph-routing instances.

Baseline comparisons confound architecture with scalarization. GMS is generally trained with Chebyshev scalarization, whereas MBM and several classical baselines use linear scalarization; linear scalarization cannot recover unsupported Pareto solutions. Matched-scalarization or matched-budget comparisons are needed for convincing hypervolume claims.

The strongest result, on MGMOTSPTW, lacks a strong problem-specific classical baseline. The implicit LKH/OR-Tools variants ignore time windows, while the evolutionary baselines are custom, incompletely specified, and perform extremely poorly at larger sizes. MOCVRP likewise lacks a competitive classical solver.

Results report only mean hypervolume over one apparent training run, without standard deviations, confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity across random seeds. This is insufficient for assessing the reliability of stochastic reinforcement-learning comparisons.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code or model release, and important details are missing, including the Chebyshev ideal points, the exact hypervolume normalization, random seeds, hypernetwork configuration, tanh-clipping constant, scalar-cost scaling, and precise sampling or greedy decisions during inference.

The stated O(MN^4) complexity for GMS-EB appears inconsistent with scoring only O(MN) outgoing edges per step: N construction steps and N POMO rollouts would give O(MN^3). The scalability argument therefore needs correction or a more explicit accounting of implementation costs.

On additive MGMOTSP, learned pruning is only marginally better than simple post-encoder pruning. Its substantial advantage is demonstrated mainly on one synthetic time-window construction, and broader architectural ablations are absent.

Overall, the problem and model ideas are promising, but the fairness, statistical rigor, real-world relevance, and reproducibility of the evaluation leave the paper slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

The learned-versus-simple-versus-pre-pruning ablations, additional neural baselines, training-time analysis, and extensive appendix materially support the architectural motivation.
weaknesses: All multigraph experiments use synthetic, fully connected FLEX/FIX instances with independent random attributes; these distributions explicitly violate the triangle inequality. The absence of a realistic road-network or established multigraph benchmark leaves the motivating practical claims insufficiently validated, and cross-distribution generalization is not tested.

Several comparisons are confounded by scalarization: the proposed models generally use Chebyshev rewards, whereas classical methods and multigraph MBM use linear scalarization, which the paper itself notes cannot recover unsupported Pareto solutions. The time-window baselines are especially disadvantaged by crude pre-pruning or by ignoring time windows, so the large gains there are not conclusive against a strong specialized solver.

The stated O(MN^4) decoding complexity for GMS-EB appears incorrect under the paper's own description: O(MN) outgoing candidates across O(N) steps and O(N) POMO trajectories gives O(MN^3), assuming fixed embedding dimension. This weakens part of the theoretical scalability motivation, although the empirical runtime difference remains clear.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence are incomplete: the manuscript does not specify the Chebyshev ideal values, exact hypervolume normalization, important decoder and hypernetwork details, random seeds, or repeated-training variation. No confidence intervals are reported despite several close comparisons, and no usable implementation artifact is identified.

Training is expensive—up to roughly 1.7 GPU-hours per epoch for GMS-EB on the reported multigraph setting—and total compute across separately trained problem/distribution configurations is not quantified. GMS-DH also has a structural limitation because it selects edges before knowing the partial route, with degradation already visible for more parallel edges and some tri-objective settings.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and potentially useful setting: neural multi-objective routing on multigraphs. The two proposed approaches offer a sensible quality-efficiency tradeoff: GMS-EB directly models edge actions, while GMS-DH introduces learned, preference-conditioned pruning followed by node-based routing.
The experiments cover several routing variants, graph sizes, numbers of parallel edges, asymmetric distributions, zero-shot size generalization, and two- versus three-objective settings.

Against the selected neural and evolutionary baselines, the methods are often substantially better and approach the solution quality of LKH or HGS while offering faster amortized inference in some regimes.
The appendices provide useful architectural descriptions, training-time measurements, additional baselines, and some pruning ablations.
weaknesses: The empirical setting does not substantiate the paper's practical motivation. All multigraphs are synthetic dense graphs with independent uniform attributes; FIX artificially sorts attributes, and neither distribution is metric. There are no real road networks or realistically correlated time-distance alternatives. The time-window task additionally forbids waiting, departing significantly from standard routing practice.

The comparisons are materially confounded. GMS is generally trained with Chebyshev scalarization, whereas pre-pruned neural baselines and LKH/HGS use linear scalarization, which cannot recover unsupported Pareto points. Thus the experiments do not cleanly isolate the benefit of multigraph-aware modeling. When strong classical solvers are included, LKH or HGS still gives the best hypervolume.

The flagship time-window experiment uses only MOEA/D and an ad hoc pre-pruned neural baseline in the main comparison. It lacks a competitive time-window heuristic, exact reference on small instances, or an adaptation of modern constrained neural routing methods, so its large reported margins are not convincing evidence of state-of-the-art performance.

There is no statistical assessment: training seeds, repeated runs, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are absent. Several claimed gains are below one hypervolume percentage point, and no validation or checkpoint-selection protocol is described.

The stated complexity analysis appears incorrect. Given the paper's claim that GMS-EB scores only the O(MN) edges leaving the current node, N construction steps and N POMO trajectories imply O(MN^3), not O(MN^4). Moreover, GMS-DH still encodes and stores O(MN^2) edge representations before pruning, so its claimed memory scalability is not established asymptotically.

Runtime comparisons mix an A40 GPU for neural methods with CPUs for classical methods and exclude substantial training costs. The reported per-epoch figures imply roughly 80 GPU-hours for a 200-epoch GMS-DH multigraph model and about 340 GPU-hours for GMS-EB, while augmented GMS-EB can be as slow as or slower than LKH. Equal-budget quality-runtime curves are needed.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the numerical ideal point used by the Chebyshev reward, the precise hypervolume normalization, hypernetwork architecture, clipping constant, CVRP depot and feasibility masks, tri-objective preference sampling, full MOEA settings, random seeds, and source code or checkpoints.

The ablations do not adequately validate the technical design. There are no controlled tests of shared encoding, the edge-cost score term, collaborative two-head training, curriculum, or K1/K2. Learned pruning is not compared with an oracle, and the highly degraded pre-pruning variant is itself confounded by different data flow and scalarization.

Overall, the problem formulation and models are plausible, but the combination of artificial evaluation, inadequate controls and baselines, missing uncertainty, reproducibility gaps, and the complexity error constitutes multiple major weaknesses rather than the minor deficiencies appropriate for a borderline acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant and comparatively underexplored problem—neural multi-objective routing on directed multigraphs—and proposes two complementary architectures with explicit quality-versus-speed tradeoffs. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/r-3b30f255031c4d37/reviews/review-experiment-sp09yw_9/call-7e974a59115a418ab9c3f7df88d7925e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The designs are coherent: GMS-EB directly selects edges, while GMS-DH combines permutation-invariant edge encoding, learned pruning, and node-based routing. The joint reinforcement-learning formulation is technically plausible.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering TSP, CVRP, and time-window variants; multiple graph distributions; two and three objectives; up to 200 nodes and ten parallel edges; runtime, zero-shot, augmentation, training-cost, and pruning ablations.

Results are consistently competitive on the tested synthetic distributions. In many settings, the models approach strong LKH/HGS solutions while providing substantially faster amortized inference, and the faster GMS-DH generally preserves reasonable solution quality.
weaknesses: The claimed practical relevance is not substantiated: every experiment uses synthetic complete graphs. FLEX/FIX use independent artificial edge attributes and explicitly violate the triangle inequality, while no sparse road network, real multigraph, or standard application dataset is evaluated.

The central learned-pruning contribution receives weak evidence. For additive MGMOTSP, exact simple pruning is available and nearly matches learned pruning in Table 5. On the only clearly context-dependent problem, MGMOTSPTW, the comparison is against weak evolutionary methods and deliberately naive pruning; there is no strong problem-specific heuristic, exact small-instance reference, or natural per-step node-then-edge neural baseline.

Comparisons conflate important factors: GMS generally uses Chebyshev rewards while several baselines use linear scalarization; MOEAs have ad hoc iteration/local-search limits and are acknowledged to perform poorly; GPU and CPU runtimes are compared across different hardware; and the very large model-training cost is excluded from efficiency claims.

Statistical evidence is inadequate. Results apparently come from one training run, with no seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests. Consequently, many sub-percent differences and ablation conclusions are not reliable.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code and missing consequential details, including the Chebyshev ideal point and objective normalization, normalized-HV formula, hypernetwork architecture, tanh-clipping constant, inference decision rule, and complete configurations for classical solvers.

The technical novelty is moderate because most components are adaptations of GREAT, POMO, hypernetworks, and multi-pointer decoding. Moreover, the stated O(MN^4) complexity for GMS-EB appears inconsistent with scoring only O(MN) outgoing edges over N steps and N POMO trajectories, which would give O(MN^3); the full scalability analysis is therefore unclear.
